meta.title: Claude Fable 5.1 vs DeepSeek R1: Which one to choose in 2026? (models, context & API pricing & code compared)
meta.description: Compare Claude Fable 5.1 and DeepSeek R1 architectural trade-offs, context windows, model APIs, and integration, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Claude Fable 5.1 is a strong fit for long-context production workloads that need a very large context window (up to 1M tokens), high output capacity up to 128K tokens, and Anthropic's managed API with prompt caching. DeepSeek R1 is better when open-weight availability, self-hosting, or very low per-token cost matter more than the largest context window. Verify current DeepSeek R1 specs and pricing against official documentation before committing, because they are version- and date-sensitive.

comparison.toolA: Claude Fable 5.1 provides a 1M-token context window and a 128K maximum output, per Anthropic's official model documentation. This supports very long documents, large codebases, and multi-turn conversations that would exceed smaller windows. Actual usable context depends on the request structure and any provider-side limits.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1's context window and maximum output are specified in DeepSeek's official model documentation and should be checked there for the exact R1 version and deployment. As an open-weight family, the deployed context window can also depend on the serving stack used by a third-party provider. The window is generally smaller than Fable 5.1's 1M tokens, but the exact figure needs verification.

comparison.category: Benchmark performance (MMLU, HumanEval, and comparable published results)
comparison.toolA: Anthropic publishes model evaluations, but scores vary by evaluation setup and prompt format, so Fable 5.1's MMLU and HumanEval results should be taken from the official model card and compared only when the methodology matches. Independent scores are not interchangeable across providers. Treat any single-number comparison as indicative, not definitive.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek has published benchmark results for the R1 family, including reasoning-oriented evaluations, in its official papers and model cards. Scores depend on the R1 version, decoding settings, and whether tools or chain-of-thought prompting are used. For a fair comparison, confirm that the same benchmark version and evaluation harness are being used for both models.

comparison.toolA: Claude Fable 5.1 base API pricing is $10 per 1M input tokens and $50 per 1M output tokens, per Anthropic's official pricing documentation. Prompt-cache reads cost $0.25 per 1M tokens, which is 97.5% below the base input price. Prices and availability may change, so confirm current rates before budgeting.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1's API pricing varies by provider and by whether you use DeepSeek's first-party API or a third-party host. DeepSeek has historically positioned R1 pricing below frontier closed models, but exact per-1M input and output figures must be verified against DeepSeek's current pricing page. Self-hosting shifts cost to infrastructure rather than per-token billing.

comparison.toolA: Claude Fable 5.1 latency depends on prompt length, output length, region, and load; Anthropic does not publish a single guaranteed latency number. Long-context requests and high output limits can increase time-to-first-token and total response time. Measure latency in your own environment under representative load.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1 is a reasoning-oriented model, and reasoning models often generate longer internal traces before answering, which can increase latency. Actual latency depends on the hosting provider, hardware, batching, and whether reasoning output is exposed. Self-hosting can reduce network overhead but adds operational tuning work.

comparison.toolA: Claude Fable 5.1 is a closed model available through Anthropic's managed API and related platform channels. Access requires an Anthropic account, accepted terms, and any applicable usage limits for your tier. You do not get model weights, so deployment options are limited to supported endpoints.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1 is distributed as open-weight models under a published license, and is also available through DeepSeek's API and third-party hosts. Open weights enable self-hosting, fine-tuning, and data-residency control, subject to the license terms. Check the specific R1 variant's license and hardware requirements before planning a deployment.

comparison.toolA: Claude Fable 5.1 suits long-document analysis, large-codebase review, multi-step agent workflows, and enterprise applications that benefit from a managed API, prompt caching, and a 1M-token window. Teams already using Anthropic tooling can integrate it without managing infrastructure. Cost control matters at $10/$50 per 1M input/output tokens, especially for output-heavy tasks.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1 suits reasoning-heavy tasks, research prototypes, cost-sensitive batch jobs, and deployments where open weights or self-hosting are required. It can be integrated through DeepSeek's API or run on your own infrastructure, which offers flexibility but transfers operational responsibility to your team. Choose it when license compliance, data control, or unit economics outweigh managed-service convenience.

comparison.toolA: Anthropic publishes usage policies, security documentation, and data-handling terms for its API; enterprises should review the current trust center and contract terms for their region and plan. Prompt caching introduces retained cache data, so confirm retention and isolation behavior in the official documentation. Compliance certifications and regional availability can change and should be verified for your account tier.
comparison.toolB: DeepSeek R1's data handling depends heavily on the deployment: first-party API, third-party host, or self-hosted weights each carry different privacy and compliance profiles. Self-hosting gives the most control but requires your own security program. Review the model license, the host's terms, and any regional data-residency requirements before processing sensitive data.

comparison.category: Verified Claude Fable 5.1 specifications and pricing
comparison.toolA: Anthropic documents a 1M-token context window, up to 128K output tokens, and API rates of $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens for Claude Fable 5.1. Prompt-cache reads cost $0.25 per million tokens, 97.5% below the base input rate; verify current pricing before deployment.
comparison.toolB: Context limits, maximum output, and pricing for this option depend on its model, provider, and service terms. Do not transfer Claude specifications to it; check the provider's current official documentation before deployment.

faq.q: Which model has the larger context window?
faq.a: Claude Fable 5.1 has a documented 1M-token context window and a 128K maximum output, which is larger than what DeepSeek R1 typically offers. DeepSeek R1's exact context window depends on the R1 version and the serving stack, so check DeepSeek's official documentation for the specific deployment. If you routinely process very long documents or codebases, Fable 5.1's window is a concrete advantage.

faq.q: Which model is cheaper for high-volume API usage?
faq.a: Claude Fable 5.1 costs $10 per 1M input tokens and $50 per 1M output tokens, with prompt-cache reads at $0.25 per 1M tokens. DeepSeek R1 pricing depends on the provider and is generally positioned lower, but you must verify current per-token rates on DeepSeek's official pricing page. For output-heavy workloads, compare effective cost per task, not just per-token price, because reasoning models can generate more tokens.

faq.q: Can I self-host Claude Fable 5.1 or DeepSeek R1?
faq.a: Claude Fable 5.1 is a closed model and is not available for self-hosting; you access it through Anthropic's managed API and supported channels. DeepSeek R1 is distributed as open-weight models, so it can be self-hosted subject to its license and your hardware capacity. Self-hosting R1 gives you data control but adds operational and compliance responsibility.

faq.q: Which model is better for coding tasks?
faq.a: Both models can handle coding, but the better choice depends on your task shape: Fable 5.1's large context window helps with repository-scale review and long specifications, while R1's reasoning focus can help with algorithmic problem solving. Published HumanEval scores are only comparable when the benchmark version and evaluation setup match, so consult each provider's official model card. For production use, validate on your own representative coding tasks.

faq.q: How should I think about latency for these models?
faq.a: Neither provider guarantees a single latency figure; latency varies with prompt length, output length, region, and load. Reasoning-oriented models like DeepSeek R1 may spend additional time generating internal reasoning before the final answer, which can raise perceived latency. Measure time-to-first-token and total response time in your own environment rather than relying on general claims.

faq.q: What benchmarks should I use to compare Fable 5.1 and DeepSeek R1?
faq.a: Use only published results that share the same benchmark version, prompt format, and evaluation harness, such as comparable MMLU or HumanEval runs from each provider's official model card. Treat cross-provider single-number comparisons as indicative because scoring methodology differs. For a decision, supplement public benchmarks with an internal evaluation set that reflects your actual workload.

faq.q: Which model should I choose for an enterprise deployment?
faq.a: Choose Claude Fable 5.1 when you need a managed API, a 1M-token context window, high output limits, prompt caching, and Anthropic's published security and compliance documentation for your region and tier. Choose DeepSeek R1 when open weights, self-hosting, data residency control, or lower per-token cost are decisive, and you can take on the operational and licensing responsibilities. In both cases, verify current pricing, terms, and feature availability against official documentation before committing.
